section.heading: 8.7. Double Integrals
A Geometric Interpretation of the Double Integral
section.paragraph: To introduce the notion of the integral of a function of two variables, let’s first recall the definition of the definite integral of a continuous function of one variable $$y = f(x)$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . We first divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals, each of equal length, by the points $$x_{0} = a < x_{1} < x_{2} < \cdots < x_{n} = b$$ and define the Riemann sum by
$$S_{n} = f\left( p_{1} \right)h + f\left( p_{2} \right)h + \cdots + f\left( p_{n} \right)h$$

where $$h = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ and $$p_{i}$$ is an arbitrary point in the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ . The definite integral of $$f$$ over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is then defined as the limit of the Riemann sum $$S_{n}$$ as $$n$$ tends to infinity, whenever it exists. Furthermore, recall that when $$f$$ is a nonnegative continuous function on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then the $$i$$ th term of the Riemann sum, $$f\left( p_{i} \right)h$$ , is an approximation (by the area of a rectangle) of the area under that part of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = x_{i - 1}$$ and $$x = x_{i}$$ , so that the Riemann sum $$S_{n}$$ provides us with an approximation of the area under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ . The integral
$$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}S_{n}}$$
gives the actual area under the curve from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ .

Now suppose $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a continuous function of two variables defined over a region $$R$$ . For simplicity, we assume for the moment that $$R$$ is a rectangular region in the plane (Figure 32). Let’s construct a Riemann sum for this function over the rectangle $$R$$ by following a procedure that parallels the case for a function of one variable over an interval $$I$$ . We begin by observing that the analog of a partition in the two-dimensional case is a rectangular grid composed of $$\mathit{mn}$$ rectangles, each of length $$h$$ and width $$k$$ , as a result of partitioning the side of the rectangle $$R$$ of length $$\left( {b - a} \right)$$ into $$m$$ segments and the side of length $$\left( {d - c} \right)$$ into $$n$$ segments. By construction,
$$h = \frac{b - a}{m}$$
and
$$k = \frac{d - c}{n}$$
A sample grid with $$m = 5$$ and $$n = 4$$ is shown in Figure 33.

section.paragraph: Let’s label the rectangles $$R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}\ldots.,R_{\mathit{mn}}$$ . If $$\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ is any point in $$R_{i}\left( {1 \leq i \leq mn} \right)$$ , then the Riemann sum of $$\mathbf{f}\left( {\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \right)$$ over the region $$\mathbf{R}$$ is defined as
$$S\left( {m,n} \right) = f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)hk + f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)hk + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( {x_{\mathit{mn}},y_{\mathit{mn}}} \right)hk$$

If the limit of $$S\left( {m,n} \right)$$ exists as both $$m$$ and $$n$$ tend to infinity, we call this limit the value of the double integral of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over the region $$R$$ and denote it by
$$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

If $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a nonnegative function, then it defines a solid $$S$$ bounded above by the graph of $$f$$ and below by the rectangular region $$R$$ . Furthermore, the solid $$S$$ is the union of the $$\mathit{mn}$$ solids bounded above by the graph of $$f$$ and below by the $$\mathit{mn}$$ rectangular regions corresponding to the partition of $$R$$ (Figure 34).

section.paragraph: Therefore, the Riemann sum $$S\left( {m,n} \right)$$ gives us an approximation of the volume of the solid bounded above by the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and below by the plane region $$R$$ . As both $$m$$ and $$n$$ tend to infinity, the Riemann sum $$S\left( {m,n} \right)$$ approaches the actual volume under the solid.
section.heading: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Rectangular Region
section.paragraph: Let’s turn our attention to the evaluation of the double integral
$$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

where $$R$$ is the rectangular region shown in Figure 32. As in the case of the definite integral of a function of one variable, it turns out that the double integral can be evaluated without our having to first find an appropriate Riemann sum and then take the limit of that sum. Instead, as we will now see, the technique calls for evaluating two single integrals—the so-called iterated integrals—in succession, using a process that might be called “antipartial differentiation.” The technique is described in the following result, which we state without proof.
Let $$R$$ be the rectangle defined by the inequalities $$a \leq x \leq b$$ and $$c \leq y \leq d$$ (see Figure 33). Then
$$\int_{R}{\int{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}dA = {\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx}} \right\rbrack dy}}}}$$
where the iterated integrals on the right-hand side are evaluated as follows. We first compute the integral
$$\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx}$$

by treating $$y$$ as if it were a constant and integrating the resulting function of $$x$$ with respect to $$x$$ ( $$\mathit{dx}$$ reminds us that we are integrating with respect to $$x$$ ). In this manner, we obtain a value for the integral that may contain the variable $$y$$ . Thus,
$$\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx = g(y)}$$
for some function $$g$$ . Substituting this value into Equation (19) gives
which may be integrated in the usual manner.

section.heading: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Plane Region
section.paragraph: Up to now, we have assumed that the region over which a double integral is to be evaluated is rectangular. In fact, however, it is possible to compute the double integral of functions over rather arbitrary regions. The next theorem, which we state without proof, expands the number of types of regions over which we may integrate.

list.item: Suppose $$g_{1}(x)$$ and $$g_{2}(x)$$ are continuous functions on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and the region $$R$$ is defined by $$R = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|g_{1}(x) \leq y \leq g_{2}(x);a \leq x \leq b} \right\}$$ . Then (20) $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {\int_{g_{1}{(x)}}^{g_{2}{(x)}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dy}} \right\rbrack dx}}}}$$ (Figure 36a). Suppose $$h_{1}(y)$$ and $$h_{2}(y)$$ are continuous functions on $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ and the region $$R$$ is defined by $$R = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|h_{1}(y) \leq x \leq h_{2}(y);c \leq y \leq d} \right\}$$ . Then (21) $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {\int_{h_{1}{(y)}}^{h_{2}{(y)}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx}} \right\rbrack dy}}}}$$ (Figure 36b).

Observe that the lower and upper limits of integration with respect to $$y$$ in Equation (20) are given by $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ and $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ . This is to be expected, since for a fixed value of $$x$$ lying between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ , $$y$$ runs between the lower curve defined by $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ and the upper curve defined by $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ (see Figure 36a). Observe, too, that in the special case when $$g_{1}(x) = c$$ and $$g_{2}(x) = d$$ , the region $$R$$ is rectangular, and Equation (20) reduces to Equation (19).
For a fixed value of $$y$$ , $$x$$ runs between $$x = h_{1}(y)$$ and $$x = h_{2}(y)$$ , giving the indicated limits of integration with respect to $$x$$ in Equation (21) (see Figure 36b).

Note that the two curves in Figure 36b are not graphs of functions of $$x$$ (use the Vertical Line Test), but they are graphs of functions of $$y$$ . It is this observation that justifies the approach leading to Equation (21).

What is an iterated integral? How is $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$ evaluated in terms of iterated integrals, where $$R$$ is the rectangular region defined by $$a \leq x \leq b$$ and $$c \leq y \leq d$$ ?
